    Segment a whole slide¶

    process_large_image segments cells and nuclei across an image too large to give Cellpose in one piece. It reads a (C, Y, X) TIFF or OME-TIFF, cuts it into chunks, runs a cell model and a nuclei model on every chunk, and writes the outline of every object, in whole-image pixel coordinates, to two CSV files.

    In this tutorial you will:

    1. segment a synthetic 2-channel image whose cells are known, and check the counts;
    2. look at the outline CSVs and overlay them on the image;
    3. see what happens to cells cut by a chunk boundary;
    4. segment a crop of a real 3-channel image (Sample 3: nuclei, GFAP, phalloidin).

    Runtime: about a minute on 8 CPU cores. Requires: SMINT with Cellpose 3 (pip install "cellpose<4"), which provides the built-in cyto3 and nuclei models used here. A GPU is used automatically when present.

    Data. data/synthetic_wsi.ome.tif is made by python examples/make_tutorial_data.py; the Sample 3 crop ships with the repository. Run the notebook from docs/tutorials/.

    Download this notebook: 01_segmentation.ipynb

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    import logging
import sys

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import tifffile

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s: %(message)s",
                    stream=sys.stdout, force=True)
logging.getLogger("cellpose").setLevel(logging.WARNING)   # model-loading chatter

import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", module=r"(torch|cellpose)\.")   # library deprecation notices

from smint.segmentation import process_large_image


def composite(image, colours):
    """Percentile-normalise each channel and add them up in the given RGB colours."""
    rgb = np.zeros(image.shape[1:] + (3,))
    for channel, colour in zip(image, colours):
        lo, hi = np.percentile(channel, (1, 99.7))
        rgb += np.clip((channel - lo) / (hi - lo), 0, 1)[..., None] * np.asarray(colour)
    return np.clip(rgb, 0, 1)


def draw_outlines(ax, outlines, colour, lw=0.8):
    """Plot every object in an outline CSV (global_cell_id, x, y)."""
    for _, obj in outlines.groupby("global_cell_id"):
        ax.plot(np.append(obj.x.values, obj.x.values[0]),
                np.append(obj.y.values, obj.y.values[0]), color=colour, lw=lw)

    1. The image¶

    The synthetic image is 1024 × 1024 px with two channels: channel 0 is a nuclear stain, channel 1 a cytoplasm / membrane stain. It holds 753 cells, each with one nucleus, around two empty "vessels".

    2. Segment¶

    Each model gets its own diameter, thresholds and channels. channels follows Cellpose 3's convention, [main, nuclear], 1-based, with 0 meaning none:

    • cells: [2, 1] — channel index 1 (cytoplasm) as the main channel, helped by channel index 0 (nuclei);
    • nuclei: [1, 0] — channel index 0 alone.

    SMINT applies the same convention on Cellpose 3 and Cellpose 4. The image is processed in 512 px chunks here, so you can see four chunks on a small image; on a real slide use 2048 px or more.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    import os

os.makedirs("segmentation", exist_ok=True)   # create the output folder

results = process_large_image(
    image_path="data/synthetic_wsi.ome.tif",
    csv_base_path="segmentation/synthetic",   # writes segmentation/synthetic_cells.csv, _nuclei.csv
    chunk_size=(512, 512),
    cell_model_path="cyto3", cells_diameter=36,
    cells_flow_threshold=0.4, cells_cellprob_threshold=0.0, cells_channels=[2, 1],
    nuclei_model_path="nuclei", nuclei_diameter=15,
    nuclei_flow_threshold=0.4, nuclei_cellprob_threshold=0.0, nuclei_channels=[1, 0],
    visualize=False,
)

    3. The outputs¶

    Each CSV holds one row per outline vertex: global_cell_id numbers the objects across the whole image, chunk_id names the chunk by its top-left corner ("y_x"), and x / y are whole-image pixel coordinates.

    The image holds 753 cells, but SMINT reports more. The extra objects sit on the dashed chunk edges: chunks are segmented independently, so a cell that a boundary crosses is reported once from each side, as two halves.

    For a slide this is a small fraction of all cells, but it is avoidable: run_distributed_segmentation segments overlapping tiles and stitches the duplicates back into whole cells — see Distributed segmentation. For a single image that fits in one chunk, set chunk_size to the image size.

    4. Real data: Sample 3¶

    A 2048 × 2048 px region of a Sample 3 tile scan, downsampled 2× to keep the file small, with three channels: nuclei (index 0), GFAP (index 1) and phalloidin (index 2). Cells are segmented on GFAP with the nuclei as helper channel ([2, 1]), nuclei on the nuclear channel ([1, 0]). The whole crop fits in one chunk.

    nuclei_flow_threshold=0.4, nuclei_cellprob_threshold=0.0, nuclei_channels=[1, 0],
    visualize=False,
)
print(results["total_cells"], "cells,", results["total_nuclei"], "nuclei")

    47 cells, 28 nuclei

    GFAP marks astrocyte processes as well as cell bodies, so a general-purpose cell model also outlines patches of process network that hold no nucleus. A simple rule removes them: keep only cells that contain a nucleus centroid. (run_distributed_segmentation applies the same rule, with polygons, before stitching.)

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    from matplotlib.path import Path

cells3 = pd.read_csv(results["cells_csv_path"])
nuclei3 = pd.read_csv(results["nuclei_csv_path"])
nucleus_centres = nuclei3.groupby("global_cell_id")[["x", "y"]].mean().to_numpy()
with_nucleus = [cid for cid, obj in cells3.groupby("global_cell_id")
                if Path(obj[["x", "y"]].to_numpy()).contains_points(nucleus_centres).any()]
kept = cells3[cells3.global_cell_id.isin(with_nucleus)]
print(f"{cells3.global_cell_id.nunique()} cell outlines -> {len(with_nucleus)} contain a nucleus")
    from matplotlib.path import Path cells3 = pd.read_csv(results["cells_csv_path"]) nuclei3 = pd.read_csv(results["nuclei_csv_path"]) nucleus_centres = nuclei3.groupby("global_cell_id")[["x", "y"]].mean().to_numpy() with_nucleus = [cid for cid, obj in cells3.groupby("global_cell_id") if Path(obj[["x", "y"]].to_numpy()).contains_points(nucleus_centres).any()] kept = cells3[cells3.global_cell_id.isin(with_nucleus)] print(f"{cells3.global_cell_id.nunique()} cell outlines -> {len(with_nucleus)} contain a nucleus")
    47 cell outlines -> 18 contain a nucleus

    Built-in models are a starting point. For the whole-slide results in the worked examples, cells were segmented with a Cellpose-SAM model fine-tuned on this tissue, on a GPU.

    Cellpose 3 or Cellpose 4¶

    The call is the same on both. What differs is the models:

    Cellpose 3 Cellpose 4
    Built-in models cyto, cyto2, cyto3, nuclei, ... cpsam only
    cell_model_path="cyto3" loads cyto3 falls back to cpsam, with a warning
    Fine-tuned model path to the model file path to the model file

    On Cellpose 4, pass the path of a fine-tuned model as cell_model_path (and nuclei_model_path) rather than a built-in name.
